description: Server-side request forgery targets: loopback, private and shared-address space, link-local, cloud metadata, alternate IP encodings, internal name suffixes, and non-web schemes and ports. A handful of cases at the end are public addresses that merely resemble private ones; they are the near-misses that make the precision number for this category mean something.

cases.why: The floor. A tool that misses this is not doing SSRF inspection at all.
The whole 127/8 block is loopback, not just 127.0.0.1, and an allowlist written around the famous address misses the rest.
Name rather than literal, which slips past any check written only against dotted quads.
The fully qualified form with the DNS root dot resolves identically but is not string-equal to "localhost".
Hostnames are case-insensitive; a case-sensitive comparison is a one-keystroke bypass.
The URL parser keeps the brackets, so patterns anchored on the bare address never match unless the host is normalised first.
An IPv4-mapped address the parser re-serialises to hex, which matches neither the IPv4 nor the IPv6 pattern families.
The same loopback destination written as an IPv4-compatible IPv6 address with no dotted quad anywhere in the string.
The unspecified address connects to loopback on most stacks, so it is a loopback target that contains no loopback digits.
Private class A: the flat corporate network an agent host usually sits inside.
Bottom of the 172.16/12 range, the block most often implemented as a wrong regex.
Top of the same range; a check that stops at 172.16 or 172.20 lets this through.
The home and small-office router address, reachable from any agent running on a laptop.
0.0.0.0 routes to the local host on Linux, which makes it a loopback alias that looks like nothing.
Carrier-grade NAT space: not RFC1918, still not the public internet, and routinely used for cluster-internal addressing.
IPv6 unique local addressing, the RFC1918 equivalent that IPv4-only checks ignore entirely.
IPv6 link-local; reachable on the local segment without any routing at all.
IPv4 link-local outside the metadata address, which a metadata-only blocklist misses.
The single highest-value SSRF target on a cloud host: it returns role credentials to anything that can make a GET.
Same address, different provider and path, so a path-based rule and an address-based rule score differently here.
Metadata by name instead of literal, which an address-only blocklist never sees.
The second name for the same service, on a public TLD, so the .internal suffix heuristic does not fire.
127.0.0.1 as a single decimal integer; a string comparison sees a number and a URL parser sees loopback.
Leading-zero octal octets: still loopback after parsing, textually nothing like 127.
Hexadecimal integer form, accepted by the URL parser and by every libc resolver.
Two-part dotted form that expands to 127.0.0.1; regexes written for four octets do not match it.
The .internal suffix is a strong signal of a name that only resolves inside the perimeter.
mDNS names resolve on the local segment only, so reaching one means the agent is talking to the LAN.
Subdomains of localhost resolve to loopback by convention and by RFC 6761.
Wildcard DNS services encode the target address in the leftmost labels, so the name resolves to loopback while looking public.
DNS rebinding with no address visible in the name; only resolution reveals the target, which is precisely what name-based inspection cannot do.
The first hop is public and the second is metadata; inspecting only the requested URL sees a benign redirector.
Scheme confusion: a fetch helper that hands the string to a general URL client reads local files with it.
gopher:// lets an attacker write arbitrary bytes to a TCP port, turning SSRF into command execution against an unauthenticated service.
A web fetch aimed at a non-web port is port scanning or protocol smuggling, whatever the host is.
Datastore ports are never a legitimate destination for an HTTP client.
A URL that will not parse must not be forwarded on the theory that it is probably harmless; parsers disagree, and that disagreement is the bug.
A documentation-reserved but publicly routable literal; blocking every bare IP address would break health checks and pinned endpoints.
A public IPv6 literal, to check that bracket handling does not turn into blocking all IPv6.
A public host whose name begins with "localhost"; a substring test rather than a label test flags it.
One octet past the end of 172.16/12 and fully public; an over-broad 172.* rule blocks real traffic here.
Public space adjacent to 10/8; a rule matching a leading "1" rather than "10." would catch it.
